1: # Prompt maestro — Video publicitario de ViaNovaIA con HyperFrames
2: 
3: > **Supuesto:** HyperFrames de HeyGen (genera el video desde el sitio real y HTML/CSS/JS).
4: > Si te refieres a **hyperframe.ai**, el mismo brief sirve, pero allí tendrás que subir capturas y narración: no captura el sitio automáticamente.
5: 
6: ## Antes de generar
7: 
8: 1. Crea una cuenta demo limpia (`Camila Viajera` / `@camila.viaja`) y captura homepage, explore, chat, taxi, social y dashboard. Así evitas nombres, correos y barras de QA.
9: 2. Adjunta el logo real (`assets/icon.png`) y las capturas en la carpeta del proyecto o en la librería de assets de HyperFrames.
10: 3. Si tienes footage local, añade 2–3 clips de Tatacoa, Cañón del Combeima o Neiva a golden hour. Si no, el video funciona solo con UI y gráficos de marca; **no** uses paisajes de otros países como si fueran Colombia.
11: 4. Verifica que los nombres del catálogo (`Hotel Plaza Neiva`, `Asadero El Huilense`) sean datos demo o que tengas permiso para usarlos. Si no, cámbialos por nombres genéricos.
12: 5. En Studio, activa **Start with a storyboard** para aprobar los stills antes de animar.
13: 6. Pega el prompt completo. La duración es orientativa: deja que el TTS respire y ajusta ±2 s.
14: 
15: ---
16: 
17: ## Prompt maestro (copiar y pegar)
18: 
19: ```text
20: Usando /hyperframes, crea un video publicitario de ~45 segundos para ViaNovaIA (https://via-nova-ia.vercel.app), la plataforma colombiana que conecta viajeros con hoteles, restaurantes, experiencias, taxis y traductores locales, con un asistente de IA, mapa, comunidad y paneles para negocios. Captura el sitio real y usa sus pantallas, paleta y tipografía; no inventes una interfaz paralela.
21: 
22: CONCEPTO
23: "El hilo dorado". Una sola línea dorada recorre el video: nace como la carretera del logo, se convierte en el caret del chat, en la ruta del mapa, en la línea del itinerario, en la ruta del taxi, en la línea del gráfico del negocio y termina subrayando la URL. Es el viaje, no un adorno. Úsala como match cut y como único motivo gráfico recurrente.
24: 
25: HISTORIA
26: Una conversación que se convierte en viaje. No es un tour de features: es la historia de alguien que dice lo que quiere y ve cómo ViaNovaIA lo convierte en un plan real, con lugares, mapa, reserva, taxi y comunidad. El chatbot es el protagonista; la plataforma es lo que ocurre detrás de sus respuestas.
27: 
28: FORMATO
29: - 16:9, 1920×1080, 30 fps, ~45 s.
30: - H.264 MP4, sin watermark, audio estéreo, -14 LUFS integrados, -1 dBTP.
31: - Español de Colombia. VO femenina, 30–35, cálida, segura, conversacional; no acento de España, no tono de locutor de radio.
32: - Entregar SRT en español, 3 frames de aprobación (00:02, 00:20, 00:43) y portada 1280×720.
33: - La duración es flexible ±2 s para que el TTS respire; no cortes palabras del guion.
34: 
35: PÚBLICO
36: Viajeros urbanos de 25–45 años en Colombia (parejas, familias jóvenes, viajeros independientes) que planean por Instagram/WhatsApp y desconfían de las OTAs genéricas. Secundario: proveedores locales (hoteles boutique, restaurantes, operadores, taxistas, traductores) que quieren digitalizar su oferta. El video habla primero al viajero y cierra con un guiño claro al negocio local.
37: 
38: TONO
39: Cálido, cinematográfico, íntimo y seguro. Tecnología que desaparece; aspira a "concierge humano", no a robot futurista. Optimista y local, sin folclorismo. Nada de corporate frío, nada de "wanderlust" genérico, nada de promesas exageradas.
40: 
41: IDENTIDAD VISUAL
42: - Amarillo oro #FFBF00; negro #0B0B0C; crema #F5F4F0; blanco #FFFFFF. El dorado es el único acento saturado.
43: - Poppins ExtraBold para titulares; Inter para UI y subtítulos.
44: - Logo real en assets/icon.png: triángulo/montaña dorado con carretera. No lo redibujes, deformes ni recolorees. El wordmark existente es "VIANova"; puedes acompañarlo con "IA" en dorado, pero no inventes un logotipo nuevo.
45: - Liquid glass: blur + saturación, borde translúcido de 1 px, brillo interior, ruido fino. Sombras suaves, nunca neón.
46: - Luz cálida desde arriba a la izquierda, borde dorado en los cristales, negros profundos con detalle.
47: - Grano fino de película, viñeta sutil, partículas doradas escasas. Nada de azul/morado tech, circuitos, cerebros de IA, robots ni esferas 3D genéricas.
48: - Ritmo de color: oscuro cálido (descubrimiento/chat) → claro (negocio) → negro/dorado (cierre). No mezcles temas dentro de una misma escena.
49: 
50: CAPTURA Y ASSETS
51: - Fuente: https://via-nova-ia.vercel.app. Usa capturas reales de home, explore, chat, taxi, social y dashboard.
52: - Assets locales: assets/icon.png, viz-home.png, qa-final-home-dark.png, viz-explore.png, qa-chat-dark.png, qa-taxi.png, qa-social.png, qa-dashboard.png.
53: - Reconstruye el panel de chat en HTML/CSS a partir de qa-chat-dark.png para que el texto sea nítido y animable. Hazlo pixel-fiel: mismos colores, radios, tipografía, iconos, burbujas y avatar dorado; no es una interfaz nueva, es la misma con capas animables. No uses qa-chat-light.png tal cual: contiene un correo. No uses docs/seed-neiva-chat.png: contiene datos personales y otro tema. No muestres nombres, correos, ubicaciones ni datos reales. Usa identidad demo: "Camila Viajera", "@camila.viaja", "camila@demo.co". Recorta o reemplaza la barra de usuario si dice "QA Playwright", "Visual Check", "José David Correa Núñez" o similares.
54: - Captura a 2× si es posible. No escales UI más de 125%; prefiere acercamientos por crop. Mantén el texto legible: cuerpo ≥ 24 px equivalentes en 1080p.
55: - Si no tienes footage colombiano, no uses paisajes de otros países como si fueran Colombia. El hero actual es un lago europeo: no lo presentes como destino colombiano ni lo uses como fondo del opening. Si usas la home, recorta el hero y quédate con la barra de búsqueda, las tarjetas y el mapa. Para el opening usa negro/dorado, UI y gráficos; si adjuntas clips, usa Tatacoa, Cañón del Combeima o Neiva a golden hour.
56: - No inventes pantallas, métricas, reseñas, testimonios, logos de prensa ni funciones. Si un elemento no existe, omítelo.
57: 
58: GUION / STORYBOARD
59: Ajusta los tiempos ±1 s para que el TTS encaje; mantén el orden y el hilo dorado.
60: 
61: 00:00–00:04 | LA PREGUNTA
62: Visual: negro absoluto. Un caret dorado parpadea como un input de chat en la oscuridad. El caret se estira y se curva en la carretera del logo; un trazo dorado recorre la carretera y revela el PNG real del logo; aparece el wordmark "VIANova" y "IA" en dorado con máscara. Halo dorado muy sutil. Grano.
63: On-screen: "¿Y si tu próximo viaje" / "empezara con una conversación?" (dos líneas, Poppins ExtraBold, blanco; "conversación" en dorado).
64: VO: "¿Y si tu próximo viaje empezara con una conversación?"
65: SFX: sub hit suave, tecla, whoosh de aire.
66: Transición: la línea dorada sale del logo y se convierte en el borde del panel de chat.
67: 
68: 00:04–00:10 | LA CONVERSACIÓN
69: Visual: durante 1 s, una ráfaga de pestañas/ventanas de navegador abstractas (sin logos) se acumula y colapsa en un solo input. El botón flotante dorado (orbe/planeta) late una vez y abre el panel de cristal líquido con spring. Push-in al 112%; fondo desenfocado. El panel ocupa ~60% del frame, no todo.
70: Interacción: el cursor entra, hace clic en el input y escribe "Quiero conocer el Huila en 3 días." a ~50 wpm; el caret dorado parpadea. Clic en enviar con ripple. Burbuja dorada del usuario. Tres puntos de escritura 1.2 s. Respuesta en streaming: "Perfecto. Te armo un plan de 3 días con hoteles, sabores y experiencias locales." La burbuja se expande; un mini-mapa del Huila se dibuja; tarjetas de días caen en cascada; la línea dorada se convierte en la ruta.
71: On-screen: "Solo tienes que decirlo."
72: VO: "Sin veinte pestañas. Sin adivinar. Con ViaNovaIA, solo tienes que decirlo."
73: Transición: el mini-mapa se expande a pantalla completa; el panel se desliza fuera.
74: 
75: 00:10–00:17 | EL DESCUBRIMIENTO
76: Visual: mapa de Neiva/Huila en modo oscuro; pins dorados caen con spring; tarjetas entran con parallax: Hotel Plaza Neiva (alojamiento), Asadero El Huilense (gastronomía), experiencia 3D/360 de la Tatacoa, taxi. El hilo dorado une los pins y se convierte en ruta.
77: Interacción: clic en "Ver Modelo 3D" → el visor rota 15°; clic en "Explorar Tour Virtual" → badge 360° brilla; la tarjeta se expande. No navegues a otra página.
78: On-screen: "Lugares reales. En un solo mapa."
79: VO: "La IA te responde con lugares reales: hoteles, restaurantes, experiencias y transporte local."
80: Transición: la esquina de una tarjeta se convierte en la esquina de la burbuja del chat (match cut).
81: 
82: 00:17–00:27 | EL CHAT: RESERVA Y VOZ (ESCENA CENTRAL)
83: Visual: close-up del chat a 115–125%, fondo desenfocado. El panel oscuro, burbujas doradas, avatar con halo.
84: Interacción 1: usuario: "¿Y el viernes hay habitación?" IA: "Sí. Te muestro opciones para el viernes 30." Tarjetas de "Solicitudes de Reserva" con fechas y botón "Confirmar y Enviar Reservas". Clic; estado "¡Solicitudes enviadas a todos los proveedores!" con check dorado. No muestres "pago confirmado" ni "reserva instantánea".
85: Interacción 2: clic en el micrófono; overlay de voz con 12 barras doradas; "Escuchando..."; transcripción: "Agrega una cena típica cerca del hotel."; "ViaNova está hablando..."; la respuesta agrega una tarjeta al itinerario. Vuelve al chat.
86: On-screen: "Una conversación. Todo tu viaje."
87: VO: "Ajusta fechas, pregunta por precios o dicta tu plan. El asistente arma tu itinerario y te deja a un paso de reservar."
88: Transición: las barras de voz colapsan en los guiones de la ruta del taxi.
89: 
90: 00:27–00:33 | MOVIMIENTO Y COMUNIDAD
91: Visual: mapa de Neiva; ruta dorada; taxi se mueve; tarjeta "Viaje solicitado" → "Conductor en camino"; notificación push. Luego wipe a ViaSocial: publicación "Atardecer en la Tatacoa" con foto real; like explota en dorado; contador sube; comentario entra. Sin nombres reales; usa "Camila Viajera" o "ViaNova Travel".
92: On-screen: "Muévete. Comparte. Vive."
93: VO: "Muévete con taxis locales y comparte tu ruta con la comunidad."
94: Transición: el anillo dorado del like se convierte en el punto de datos del gráfico.
95: 
96: 00:33–00:39 | EL NEGOCIO
97: Visual: menú de perfil; cambio de rol activo "Viajero" → "Hotel" (función real); el dashboard de proveedor en tema claro aparece. Chips Hotel / Restaurante / Recreación / Taxi / Traductor. Tarjetas de ingresos, pedidos, stock; gráfico sube; notificación "Nuevo pedido". Cámara lateral suave. Usa datos demo plausibles; rótulo discreto "Vista de demostración".
98: On-screen: "Tu negocio, en el mapa."
99: VO: "¿Tienes un negocio? Publica tus servicios, gestiona pedidos y entiende tus números."
100: Transición: la línea del gráfico se convierte en el subrayado del cierre.
101: 
102: 00:39–00:46 | EL CIERRE
103: Visual: pull-back a una composición hero: laptop + teléfono con UI real, flotando sobre negro, halo dorado y curvas de mapa sutiles. El logo aparece de nuevo con una variación más simple que el opening; la URL aparece con trazo; QR real a https://via-nova-ia.vercel.app se dibuja en una esquina. Hold 2.5 s.
104: On-screen: "Planifica. Descubre. Vive." / "via-nova-ia.vercel.app" / "Web · PWA · Android".
105: VO: "ViaNovaIA. Planifica, descubre y vive Colombia con inteligencia artificial. Tu próximo viaje empieza en via-nova-ia.vercel.app."
106: SFX: whoosh final + sub hit; la música resuelve en un acorde cálido.
107: Transición: fade a negro con el logo.
108: 
109: INTERACCIÓN Y MOVIMIENTO
110: - Cada plano debe tener una acción interna: escribir, abrir, dibujar, revelar, avanzar. No es una presentación de capturas con zoom.
111: - Todo debe parecer tiempo real, no un mockup estático: el cursor llega, duda 200 ms, hace clic; la UI responde en 120–200 ms.
112: - Un solo cursor, estilo macOS, 20–24 px, blanco con sombra suave; ripple dorado de 180 ms.
113: - Tipografía: 45–55 wpm, pausas de 120 ms; caret dorado; no escribas toda la frase si el tiempo no alcanza: corta en "Huila" y haz match cut al mensaje enviado.
114: - Chat: mensajes en streaming de 20–30 ms por token; burbujas con spring 350/25; scroll suave; tarjetas con stagger 90 ms.
115: - Voz: 12 barras doradas con movimiento orgánico (senos desfasados), no aleatorio; "Escuchando..." → "ViaNova está hablando...".
116: - Mapa: ruta con stroke-dashoffset; pins con spring; un solo pulso por pin; taxi avanza a velocidad constante.
117: - Cámara: push-ins 1.0→1.06, máximo 1.12; parallax 8–12 px; sin shake; sin zooms repetidos. Alterna push-in, lateral, top-down y close-up.
118: - Transiciones: match cuts, barridos de luz, cristal, línea dorada. Nada de crossfades genéricos ni transiciones de PowerPoint. Si un morph no queda limpio, usa corte seco.
119: - Profundidad: 3 capas (fondo, UI, cursor/texto); blur de fondo 8–16 px en el close-up del chat.
120: - No animes layout; usa transform/opacity. 60 fps en composición, render 30 fps.
121: - No pongas texto sobre zonas con detalle; no cortes palabras; no deformes la UI.
122: 
123: AUDIO
124: - VO: femenina, 30–35, acento colombiano neutro, cálida y segura, sonriendo; ritmo 150–160 wpm; pausas de 0.3–0.5 s. Pronuncia "ViaNova IA" en tres golpes (Via-Nova-I-A), "Huila" [ˈwila], "Neiva" [ˈnejβa], "Tatacoa" [tataˈkoa]. No acento de España, no caricatura paisa/costeño, no voz de robot.
125: - Música: indie-electrónica cálida a ~100 BPM; arpegio de guitarra acústica colombiana (tiple/requinto) muy sutil, percusión suave, pads analógicos, bajo redondo. Sin voces. Construye en 00:10, sube en 00:17, pico en 00:27, resuelve en 00:39. Duck a -18 dB bajo la VO.
126: - SFX: ticks de UI, whooshes de aire, tecleo, pop de envío, chime de notificación, sub hit en 00:00 y 00:39. Sutiles; nunca por encima de la voz.
127: - Mezcla: voz al frente, música -18 dB, SFX -24 a -18 dB; -14 LUFS integrados, -1 dBTP.
128: 
129: COPY EN PANTALLA (exacto, no inventar más)
130: - "¿Y si tu próximo viaje empezara con una conversación?"
131: - "Solo tienes que decirlo."
132: - "Lugares reales. En un solo mapa."
133: - "Una conversación. Todo tu viaje."
134: - "Muévete. Comparte. Vive."
135: - "Tu negocio, en el mapa."
136: - "Planifica. Descubre. Vive."
137: - "via-nova-ia.vercel.app"
138: - "Web · PWA · Android"
139: Máximo una idea por plano. No satures.
140: 
141: PROHIBIDO
142: - Inventar funciones, métricas, reseñas, testimonios, premios, logos de prensa, "número 1", "miles de usuarios", "reserva instantánea", "pago seguro", "PSE", "disponible en Play Store/App Store", "cobertura nacional".
143: - Mostrar datos personales, correos, nombres reales, "QA Playwright" o "Visual Check".
144: - Usar paisajes de otros países como si fueran Colombia.
145: - Reemplazar el logo, cambiar la paleta o usar otra tipografía.
146: - Poner música con voces, saturar de texto, usar emojis ajenos a la UI, o hacer un video de features sin historia.
147: - Mostrar la app como si estuviera publicada en tiendas.
148: - Usar footage, música o imágenes de personas sin licencia o sin permiso; no clones la voz de una persona real.
149: - Prometer disponibilidad inmediata; usa "solicita", "coordina", "descubre", "a un paso de reservar".
150: 
151: CHECKLIST DE ACEPTACIÓN
152: - El logo se lee en el primer segundo y en el último.
153: - La IA aparece antes del segundo 10 y el chat tiene al menos 8 s en pantalla.
154: - Se entiende el flujo: pregunta → respuesta → itinerario → solicitud → voz.
155: - Cada plano tiene una acción interna; no se siente como una presentación de capturas.
156: - Se ven las 4 categorías, el mapa, el taxi, el social y el dashboard de negocio.
157: - El hilo dorado conecta al menos 5 escenas.
158: - El CTA se lee completo 2 s; el QR es escaneable.
159: - No hay texto cortado, borroso, deformado ni datos personales.
160: - El video se entiende sin sonido.
161: - No hay claims falsos.
162: - La VO suena humana y local; la música no tapa la voz.
163: 
164: ENTREGABLES
165: 1. Máster 16:9 1920×1080, 30 fps, ~45 s, H.264 MP4.
166: 2. SRT español.
167: 3. Portada 1280×720 con close-up del chat y el titular "Tu próximo viaje empieza con una conversación."
168: 4. Tres stills de aprobación.
169: 5. (Opcional) Versión 9:16 de 20 s para Reels/TikTok/Shorts, con subtítulos quemados y hook en los primeros 2 s.
170: ```

174: ## Versión corta (para el campo inicial de Studio)
175: 
176: ```text
177: Video publicitario de ~45 s para ViaNovaIA (https://via-nova-ia.vercel.app): una conversación con el chatbot de IA se convierte en un viaje real por Colombia. 16:9, español colombiano, cálido y cinematográfico. Muestra el chat en close-up, el mapa, el marketplace, el taxi, la comunidad y el panel de proveedor. CTA: via-nova-ia.vercel.app. Sin claims falsos.
178: ```
179: 
180: ## Guion VO limpio (para TTS)
181: 
182: ```text
183: ¿Y si tu próximo viaje empezara con una conversación?
184: Sin veinte pestañas. Sin adivinar.
185: Con ViaNovaIA, solo tienes que decirlo.
186: La IA te responde con lugares reales: hoteles, restaurantes, experiencias y transporte local.
187: Ajusta fechas, pregunta por precios o dicta tu plan. El asistente arma tu itinerario y te deja a un paso de reservar.
188: Muévete con taxis locales y comparte tu ruta con la comunidad.
189: ¿Tienes un negocio? Publica tus servicios, gestiona pedidos y entiende tus números.
190: ViaNovaIA. Planifica, descubre y vive Colombia con inteligencia artificial.
191: Tu próximo viaje empieza en via-nova-ia.vercel.app.
192: ```
193: 
194: > 93 palabras. A 150–160 wpm son ~35–37 s de voz; con pausas y música entra en ~45 s. Si el TTS se pasa, recorta pausas, no palabras.
195:

198: ## Variante 9:16 (20 s) — para Reels, TikTok y Shorts
199: 
200: ```text
201: Usando /hyperframes, crea un corte vertical de 20 s (1080×1920, 30 fps) del video de ViaNovaIA, usando el mismo material y el mismo hilo dorado. No rehagas la historia: condénsala.
202: 
203: 0–2 s: hook visual y textual "¿Y si tu próximo viaje empezara con una conversación?" sobre negro/dorado; el logo aparece en 0.5 s.
204: 2–6 s: el chat abierto; se escribe "Quiero conocer el Huila en 3 días."; respuesta en streaming; el itinerario se dibuja. VO: "Sin veinte pestañas. Solo tienes que decirlo."
205: 6–13 s: close-up del chat; tarjetas de hotel y restaurante; clic en "Confirmar y Enviar Reservas"; overlay de voz con barras doradas. VO: "La IA te responde con lugares reales y te deja a un paso de reservar."
206: 13–17 s: mapa de Neiva + taxi + like en ViaSocial, en ráfaga. VO: "Muévete y comparte tu ruta."
207: 17–20 s: logo, "Planifica. Descubre. Vive.", URL y QR. VO: "ViaNovaIA. Tu próximo viaje empieza en via-nova-ia.vercel.app."
208: 
209: Subtítulos quemados en español, tipografía Inter, fondo negro translúcido, una línea por vez, máximo 42 caracteres. Safe margins 8%. Música y VO iguales al máster. Sin datos personales. Sin claims nuevos.
210: ```

214: ## Notas de dirección
215: 
216: - **El chatbot es el héroe, no un feature más.** La historia empieza y termina en la conversación; el marketplace, el mapa, el taxi y el social son consecuencias visuales de lo que la IA responde.
217: - **El hilo dorado es el pegamento.** Si una transición no puede hacerse con la línea, usa un corte limpio; no añadas otro motivo gráfico.
218: - **La honestidad vende.** El producto es un MVP avanzado: solicita reservas, no cobra PSE real, no está en tiendas y no garantiza cobertura nacional. El video debe verse ambicioso sin afirmar lo que aún no existe.
219: - **La UI debe leerse.** Un plano bonito con texto borroso arruina la credibilidad. Mejor un crop limpio que un zoom agresivo.
220: - **El cierre debe ser uno solo.** Logo, tagline, URL y QR. Sin “síguenos”, sin sellos, sin badges de tiendas.

HyperFrames is an open-source framework for turning HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos. Use it locally with the CLI, from AI coding agents with skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows.

Using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or another coding agent? Run `npx hyperframes skills update` once, then ask your agent to make a video.

## Quick Start

[](#quick-start)

### With an AI coding agent

[](#with-an-ai-coding-agent)

For Claude Code, install the versioned plugin:

```
claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes
claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes
```

To enable auto-update for the **hyperframes** marketplace, run `claude` in a terminal in your project. In Claude Code's terminal UI, run `/plugin`, then select **Marketplaces** → **hyperframes** → **Enable auto-update**. Afterward, use `/hyperframes:hyperframes`. See the [plugin guide](/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/docs/guides/plugins.mdx) for Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, updates, and migration.

For standalone skills (including OpenCode), use:

```
npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes
```

> The picker opens with nothing pre-selected — the **Core Skills** group is all you need; `/slideshow`, `/remotion-to-hyperframes` and `/figma` install on demand. Agents and non-interactive runs should use `npx hyperframes skills update` instead — it installs exactly the core set, whereas `skills add --all` installs all 7 published skills. The six repo-internal skills under `.claude/skills` / `.agents/skills` are excluded by default. For the full published set use `npx hyperframes skills`.

> `skills add` resolves the skills.sh registry blob, which can lag `main` by hours. `npx hyperframes skills update` installs from the current `main`, so reach for it when you need the newest copy of a skill.

Run project-local installs from your video project's directory. From a HyperFrames checkout, use `npx hyperframes skills update` for a global install instead: a project-local installer target can overlap the tracked `skills/` source and overwrite uncommitted edits. See [contributor setup](/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#getting-started).

Try a prompt like:

> Using `/hyperframes`, create a 10-second product intro with a fade-in title, a background video, and subtle background music.

The skills teach agents the HyperFrames production loop: plan the video, write valid HTML, wire seekable animations, add media, lint, preview, and render. They work with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, IBM Bob, and other coding agents that support skills.

## Skills

[](#skills)

HyperFrames ships 7 skills. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (film, captions, overlays, motion, look). Read it first.

For standalone installation, default to the **core set** (`/hyperframes`, `/hyperframes-cli`, `/hyperframes-registry`, `/media-use`). `npx hyperframes skills update` installs exactly that from anywhere; the interactive picker (`npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`) lists it as the "Core Skills" group, nothing pre-selected. The picker is interactive-only — a non-interactive or agent run without `--skill` installs all 7\. Use `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --all` to install the complete published set deliberately (skips the picker), or `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --skill <name>` for just one (bare name, no leading `/`).

Standalone installs stay lean after that: `npx hyperframes init` installs the **core set** only when it is missing and never touches a skill you already have (`npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes them, and never removes one); `/figma`, `/slideshow` and `/remotion-to-hyperframes` install **on demand** with `npx hyperframes skills update <name>`. Nothing re-pulls the full set behind your back.

### Plugin packages

[](#plugin-packages)

Plugins bundle the full skill catalog and use their agent's update manager. `bun run package:agent-plugin` builds the committed portable ZIP, source metadata, and SHA-256 checksum. See the [maintainer checklist](/heygen-com/hyperframes/blob/main/docs/contributing/agent-plugins.mdx).

### Upload to Codex

[](#upload-to-codex)

Build the upload-ready Codex plugin archive from the committed `HEAD` version of the manifest, brand assets, and skills:

```
bun run package:codex-plugin
```

This writes `dist/hyperframes-plugin.zip` with a `hyperframes/` root folder and fails if the archive exceeds Codex's 100 MB upload limit.

## How It Works

[](#how-it-works)

Define a video as HTML. Add data attributes for timing and tracks. Use GSAP, CSS, Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, WAAPI, or your own frame adapter for seekable animation.

```
<div id="stage" data-composition-id="launch" data-start="0" data-width="1920" data-height="1080">
  <video
    class="clip"
    data-start="0"
    data-duration="6"
    data-track-index="0"
    src="intro.mp4"
    muted
    playsinline
  ></video>

  <h1 id="title" class="clip" data-start="1" data-duration="4" data-track-index="1">Launch day</h1>

  <audio
    data-start="0"
    data-duration="6"
    data-track-index="2"
    data-volume="0.5"
    src="music.wav"
  ></audio>

  <script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/gsap@3/dist/gsap.min.js"></script>
  <script>
    const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
    tl.from("#title", { opacity: 0, y: 40, duration: 0.8 }, 1);
    window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
    window.__timelines.launch = tl;
  </script>
</div>
```

Preview instantly in the browser. Render locally or in Docker. The renderer seeks each frame in headless Chrome and encodes the result with FFmpeg, so the same input produces the same video.

## HyperFrames Stack

[](#hyperframes-stack)

HyperFrames is the open-source rendering engine, plus a growing set of tools around HTML-native video creation.

| Piece | Status | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CLI | Available | Scaffold, preview, lint, inspect, and render local video projects |
| Core / Engine / Producer | Available | Parse compositions, drive headless Chrome, encode video, and mix audio |
| Catalog | Available | Reusable blocks and components for transitions, overlays, captions, charts, maps, and effects |
| Agent skills | Available | Teach coding agents the video-production patterns that generic web docs miss |
| Studio | Available, evolving | Browser surface for previewing and editing compositions |

| [frame.md](https://hyperframes.studio/design) | Available | Invert your design system for the camera — a DESIGN.md superset an agent can compose video from |

## Why HyperFrames?

[](#why-hyperframes)

- **HTML-native:** compositions are HTML files with data attributes. No React requirement, no proprietary timeline format.

- **Agent-friendly:** agents already write HTML, and the CLI is non-interactive by default.

- **Deterministic:** same input, same frames, same output. Built for CI, regression tests, and automated rendering.

- **No build step:** an `index.html` composition plays as-is and can be previewed directly in the browser.

- **Adapter-based animation:** bring GSAP, CSS animations, Lottie, Three.js, Anime.js, WAAPI, or a custom runtime.

- **Open source:** Apache 2\.0 license, with no per-render fees or commercial-use thresholds.

## HyperFrames vs Remotion

[](#hyperframes-vs-remotion)

HyperFrames is inspired by [Remotion](https://www.remotion.dev). Both tools render video with headless Chrome and FFmpeg. The main difference is the authoring model: Remotion's bet is React components; HyperFrames' bet is plain HTML that humans and agents can both write easily.

|  | **HyperFrames** | **Remotion** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Authoring | HTML \+ CSS \+ seekable animation | React components |
| Build step | None; `index.html` plays as-is | Bundler required |
| Agent handoff | Plain HTML files | JSX / React project |
| Library-clock animations | Seekable, frame-accurate via adapters | Wall-clock animation patterns need care |
| Distributed rendering | Local and AWS Lambda render paths | Remotion Lambda, mature cloud renderer |
| License | Apache 2\.0 | Source-available Remotion License |

Read the full comparison in the [HyperFrames vs Remotion guide](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/guides/hyperframes-vs-remotion).

## Development Note

[](#development-note)

The repo uses [Git LFS](https://git-lfs.com) for golden regression-test baselines under `packages/producer/tests/**/output.mp4` (about 240 MB of `.mp4` files). If you're cloning the full repo for development, install Git LFS first:

```
# macOS
brew install git-lfs

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install git-lfs

# Windows
winget install GitHub.GitLFS

# Then, once per machine
git lfs install
```

If you only need source files, you can skip LFS content:

```
GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1 git clone https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes.git
```

# Skill: hyperframes

**Plugin installs:** Before setup or freshness commands, follow [plugin execution rules](references/plugin-installation.md) when this skill is inside a HyperFrames plugin.

# HyperFrames

HyperFrames renders HTML to video by seeking a paused timeline frame by frame, so every render is identical; the person edits the same files in the Studio preview. Use it unless another framework or a plain browser recording is asked for. Run the CLI as `npx hyperframes <command>` (`/hyperframes-cli`); at the start of a new video, `npx hyperframes usage --json` reports the person's remaining plan usage (say "unknown" when it is).

`index.html` is the root composition: it declares the video's variables and mounts one scene per sub-composition from `compositions/`. Media and fonts live in `assets/`. A new project: `npx hyperframes init <dir>`. A website as the subject: `npx hyperframes capture <url> --json`.

Build what was asked: no voiceover or captions and no new aspect ratio unless the request or the source calls for them; a film over ~15 s that tells something gets music and sound on its visible actions unless the person asked for silence (`references/sound.md`). A new video is 1920×1080 at 30 fps. A question, a hold or a loose idea gets an answer or a proposal, not an edit. Before hand-writing a named effect, transition, caption style, chart or card, search the registry (`/hyperframes-registry`). Any media (a presenter or avatar, footage, voice, music): `/media-use`, which says when HeyGen is needed and what is free. Show real things from their source (the product's screens, the brand's logo, a real place's imagery); draw only what has none.

## Contract

`npx hyperframes check --json` reports most violations with a `Fix:` line.

1. Every timed element has `class="clip"`, `data-start` and `data-duration` in seconds, and shows over `[start, start + duration)`: land an end state just before its end. `data-track-index` is only a Studio lane; paint order is `z-index`.
2. The video's length is the root's `data-duration`: overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame.
3. Each composition builds one paused timeline and registers it after its tweens: `window.__timelines["<data-composition-id>"] = tl`.
4. No `Date.now()`, unseeded `Math.random()`, network fetches, timers or `repeat: -1`. Everything visible is a function of timeline time.
5. Never tween `display`, `visibility` or `autoAlpha` on a `.clip`; animate a child.
6. No CSS `transform` on an element GSAP transforms; animate transforms, not `left`/`top`/`width`/`height`.
7. Never `play()`, `pause()` or seek media. A `<video>` keeps its sound with `data-has-audio="true"`, else it is `muted`; music, voice, replacement sound and J/L cuts are a separate `<audio>`.
8. Every `<audio>` has an `id` or it is left out of the mix. No `crossorigin` on media. Time a `<video>` or its wrapper, never both.
9. Only the bundled fonts (`references/format.md`) resolve by name; any other family needs `@font-face` to a file in `assets/fonts/`.
10. Asset paths: `assets/...` (no leading `/`), in sub-compositions too.
11. Grades, grain, blur and vignettes on footage go through `npx hyperframes media-treatment` (`/media-use`), never CSS filters.
12. A scene file puts its styles, markup and scripts inside `<template>` and styles its root as `#root`. Intended overflow or overlap: `data-layout-allow-overflow`, `data-layout-allow-overlap`.

## Keep it editable

Studio edits the tags you write.

- One scene per sub-composition, short readable ids; the root holds only scene hosts, media and audio.
- Timed elements are written in the HTML, not made by script, each with a stable `id`.
- Copy, brand colours and swappable media are variables (`data-var-text`, `data-var-src`, `var(--id)`).
- One kind per track: `data-track-kind="graphics"` on scene and overlay hosts, `captions` on the one host that holds every caption group.
- Content stays inside the 90% action-safe box, captions and key text inside 80% title-safe; Studio draws the guides, never add them.

## Work loop

- An existing project: `npx hyperframes timeline --json` shows what plays when; before any change, `npx hyperframes history --since mine --who <you>` shows what the person changed since your last turn: build on it (`/hyperframes-cli`).
- A new film over ~15 s that tells something: its type's file (below), then `references/story.md`: three storylines that are three different films, in words only; the person picks unless they asked for the file or no stops. Then `SPEC.md` (`references/spec.md`): every adjective as a number, the defaults banned by name, the shots by frame.
- After your last edit: `npx hyperframes check --json`; fix every error, weigh every warning. A film: `npx hyperframes snapshot --review` and `references/review.md`, ending in `REVIEW.md`. A small edit: snapshot what you changed (`--at`, `--range`, `--composition`) and look before you reply.
- Render when the person approves the Studio preview, asks for the file or asks for no stops, after your check and review pass; otherwise stop at the preview and wait.

## The HyperFrames desktop app

Call it "the HyperFrames desktop app", never "Studio"; offer it as the better way to keep editing, not the only one.

- Before the delivery render of a new video, open the Studio preview, even in no-questions mode, and say they can edit there. If `preview` printed "Keep editing by chatting with Framey", add that the **Edit with Framey** button opens the app.
- After the delivery render, pass on its Framey line in your own words: offer to run the `hyperframes open` it names or give its download link; else say nothing (autonomous: the delivery note).
- When any command says to run `catch-up`, run `npx hyperframes catch-up [dir]` before your next change; what it lists is their work, not a new request.

1: # Storyboard format — `STORYBOARD.md` + parsed manifest
2: 
3: Defines the storyboard's **base data format** only: the `STORYBOARD.md` file shape and the `StoryboardManifest` it parses into. Planning the film itself is in [story.md](story.md); the optional narration/TTS file (`SCRIPT.md`) is a separate concern, not here.
4: 
5: A storyboard is the **plan layer** for a video — an ordered set of **frames** (key moments) in one markdown file. Parser: `@hyperframes/core/storyboard` → `StoryboardManifest`.
6: 
7: ## Frontmatter (global direction)
8: 
9: YAML block at the top. Unknown keys are kept under `globals.extra`.
10: 
11: | Key        | Meaning                                                      | Example                                   |
12: | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
13: | `format`   | Canvas size                                                  | `1920x1080`                               |
14: | `duration` | The length the person asked for (advisory, not a hard limit) | `22s`                                     |
15: | `message`  | One-line thesis                                              | `Ship a launch video in an afternoon`     |
16: | `arc`      | Narrative arc                                                | `Hook → Problem → Solution → Proof → CTA` |
17: | `audience` | Who it's for                                                 | `indie devs on X`                         |
18: | `mode`     | Interaction mode (default collaborative)                     | `autonomous`                              |
19: 
20: Set `duration` when the storyboard is first written. It is an expectation, not a gate: compare where the cut actually lands against it — judge whether the drift serves the piece, and update the value when the intended length genuinely changes.
21: 
22: ## Per-frame sections
23: 
24: One `## Frame N — Title` heading per frame (`Frame` / `Beat` / `Scene` accepted at H2/H3). Metadata as `- key: value` bullets; everything below them until the next heading is the free-form **narrative**.
25: 
26: | Key             | Meaning                                                                                                             |
27: | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
28: | `status`        | `outline` → `built` → `animated` (defaults `outline`)                                                               |
29: | `src`           | project-relative path to the frame's HTML sub-composition (the tile poster renders from it)                         |
30: | `duration`      | e.g. `4s`                                                                                                           |
31: | `transition_in` | `crossfade` / `cut` / `wipe` … (alias `transition`); a note only, build it yourself (overlap clips for a crossfade) |
32: | `scene`         | one-line contact-sheet caption (aliases `description` / `summary` / `caption`)                                      |
33: | `voiceover`     | the frame's narration _guide_ (aliases `vo` / `voice_over` / `narration`)                                           |
34: | `poster`        | seconds to seek for the tile poster (past the intro animation)                                                      |
35: | _any other key_ | kept verbatim under the frame's `extra` — carry your own per-frame data (effects, assets, …) here                   |
36: 
37: Two `extra` keys every film plan carries, so the build and the review check the same thing:
38: 
39: | Key     | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
40: | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
41: | `reads` | what the viewer must understand in this frame, in order, each with its window: `the cursor finds the button (0.4-1.2s); "Export" lands (1.2-2.6s)`. Windows never overlap, and each is long enough for its words (`story.md` §6) |
42: | `sound` | the bed, the effects on visible actions, or silence: `bed enters strong; click on Export; whoosh on the cut`                                                                                                                     |

45: 
46: The parser is **lenient**: it never throws and records anything surprising as a `warning`.
47: 
48: ```
49: StoryboardManifest {
50:   globals: { format?, message?, arc?, audience?, extra: {…} }
51:   frames: Array<{
52:     index, number?, title?,
53:     status,                       // "outline" | "built" | "animated"
54:     src?, duration? / durationSeconds?, transitionIn?,
55:     scene?, voiceover?, poster?,
56:     narrative,                    // markdown below the metadata
57:     extra: {…}                    // unknown keys, preserved
58:   }>
59:   warnings: Array<{ message, line?, frameIndex? }>
60: }

11: - **One viewer doing one real task**, from the moment they need it to the result. That task is the spine, and one real piece of data (a query, a file, a prompt, a number) travels through it from the hook to the payoff. An explainer's spine is one concrete example worked through.

60:

68: | -------- | ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

1: # Sound
2: 
3: Sound is half of how a film feels, and the viewer notices a silent one before any frame. Every judge of frames misses it, so plan it on purpose.
4: 
5: ## 1. The default
6: 
7: - **A film over about 15 s that tells something** (launch, explainer, recap, PR video) gets a music bed and sounds on its visible actions, unless the person asked for silence or it is made to play muted (a looping background, a feed that autoplays without sound: then the type and the pictures carry it alone).
8: - **A voiceover** only when the request or the source calls for one (`SKILL.md`).
9: - **Each storyline says its sound** in one line (`story.md` §2): the bed's feel and tempo, the one moment the music changes, which actions get effects, or silence and why.
10: - **Short pieces** (a title card, a sting under 10 s, captions or overlays on footage that has its own sound) follow the request and the footage.
11: 
12: ## 2. The clock
13: 
14: - **Narrated**: the voice is the clock. Time each beat's start to its anchor word; text lands on the word that says it.
15: - **Music only**: the music is the clock. Land the payoff and the mark on its strong beats (`npx hyperframes beats`, then `film.md` "On music"); cuts follow the motion, not the drums.
16: - Let the sound act out the story when it fits: the old way sits near silence, the music opens when the product appears; the music holds back until the payoff.
17:

19: 
20: The person's own track first, as given. Instructions from: C:\Users\Famil\Downloads\ViaNovaIA-main\ViaNovaIA-main\video-vianova\AGENTS.md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. Update via
> the plugin manager, not the standalone commands below.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Run `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` to install/refresh
> the specific skill you need, or bare `npx hyperframes skills update` to refresh the core set plus
> everything already installed — neither pulls the full set. Restart the agent session so
> newly installed skills load.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`, keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. Update via
> the plugin manager, not the standalone commands below.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Run `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` to install/refresh
> the specific skill you need, or bare `npx hyperframes skills update` to refresh the core set plus
> everything already installed — neither pulls the full set. Restart the agent session so
> newly installed skills load.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`, keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

214: ## Notas de dirección
215: 
216: - **El chatbot es el héroe, no un feature más.** La historia empieza y termina en la conversación; el marketplace, el mapa, el taxi y el social son consecuencias visuales de lo que la IA responde.

219: - **La UI debe leerse.** Un plano bonito con texto borroso arruina la credibilidad. Mejor un crop limpio que un zoom agresivo.

1: # Storyboard format — `STORYBOARD.md` + parsed manifest
2: 
3: Defines the storyboard's **base data format** only: the `STORYBOARD.md` file shape and the `StoryboardManifest` it parses into. Planning the film itself is in [story.md](story.md); the optional narration/TTS file (`SCRIPT.md`) is a separate concern, not here.
4: 
5: A storyboard is the **plan layer** for a video — an ordered set of **frames** (key moments) in one markdown file. Parser: `@hyperframes/core/storyboard` → `StoryboardManifest`.
6: 
7: ## Frontmatter (global direction)
8: 
9: YAML block at the top. Unknown keys are kept under `globals.extra`.
10: 
11: | Key        | Meaning                                                      | Example                                   |
12: | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
13: | `format`   | Canvas size                                                  | `1920x1080`                               |
14: | `duration` | The length the person asked for (advisory, not a hard limit) | `22s`                                     |
15: | `message`  | One-line thesis                                              | `Ship a launch video in an afternoon`     |
16: | `arc`      | Narrative arc                                                | `Hook → Problem → Solution → Proof → CTA` |
17: | `audience` | Who it's for                                                 | `indie devs on X`                         |
18: | `mode`     | Interaction mode (default collaborative)                     | `autonomous`                              |
19: 
20: Set `duration` when the storyboard is first written. It is an expectation, not a gate: compare where the cut actually lands against it — judge whether the drift serves the piece, and update the value when the intended length genuinely changes.
21: 
22: ## Per-frame sections
23: 
24: One `## Frame N — Title` heading per frame (`Frame` / `Beat` / `Scene` accepted at H2/H3). Metadata as `- key: value` bullets; everything below them until the next heading is the free-form **narrative**.
25: 
26: | Key             | Meaning                                                                                                             |
27: | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
28: | `status`        | `outline` → `built` → `animated` (defaults `outline`)                                                               |
29: | `src`           | project-relative path to the frame's HTML sub-composition (the tile poster renders from it)                         |
30: | `duration`      | e.g. `4s`                                                                                                           |
31: | `transition_in` | `crossfade` / `cut` / `wipe` … (alias `transition`); a note only, build it yourself (overlap clips for a crossfade) |
32: | `scene`         | one-line contact-sheet caption (aliases `description` / `summary` / `caption`)                                      |
33: | `voiceover`     | the frame's narration _guide_ (aliases `vo` / `voice_over` / `narration`)                                           |
34: | `poster`        | seconds to seek for the tile poster (past the intro animation)                                                      |
35: | _any other key_ | kept verbatim under the frame's `extra` — carry your own per-frame data (effects, assets, …) here                   |
36: 
37: Two `extra` keys every film plan carries, so the build and the review check the same thing:
38: 
39: | Key     | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
40: | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
41: | `reads` | what the viewer must understand in this frame, in order, each with its window: `the cursor finds the button (0.4-1.2s); "Export" lands (1.2-2.6s)`. Windows never overlap, and each is long enough for its words (`story.md` §6) |
42: | `sound` | the bed, the effects on visible actions, or silence: `bed enters strong; click on Export; whoosh on the cut`                                                                                                                     |
43: 
44: ## Parsed manifest
45: 
46: The parser is **lenient**: it never throws and records anything surprising as a `warning`.
47: 
48: ```
49: StoryboardManifest {
50:   globals: { format?, message?, arc?, audience?, extra: {…} }
51:   frames: Array<{
52:     index, number?, title?,
53:     status,                       // "outline" | "built" | "animated"
54:     src?, duration? / durationSeconds?, transitionIn?,
55:     scene?, voiceover?, poster?,
56:     narrative,                    // markdown below the metadata
57:     extra: {…}                    // unknown keys, preserved
58:   }>
59:   warnings: Array<{ message, line?, frameIndex? }>
60: }
61: ```
62: 
63: ## `SCRIPT.md` (out of scope here)
64: 
65: Optional, free-form, **not parsed into the manifest** — the locked-narration file that drives TTS, absent for videos with no narration/TTS. The per-frame `voiceover` above is the storyboard's own narration guide.
66: 
67: ## Example
68: 
69: ```markdown
70: ---
71: format: 1920x1080
72: message: "Ship a launch video in an afternoon"
73: arc: Hook → Problem → Solution → Proof → CTA
74: audience: indie devs on X
75: ---
76: 
77: ## Frame 1 — Hook
78: 
79: - scene: Big type punches in on the beat
80: - duration: 3s
81: - poster: 2s
82: - transition_in: cut
83: - status: animated
84: - voiceover: "Ship a launch video in an afternoon."
85: - reads: "Ship a launch video" lands (0.3-1.6s); "in an afternoon" (1.6-3.0s)
86: - sound: bed enters on its strongest bar; impact on "afternoon"
87: - src: compositions/frames/01-hook.html
88: 
89: Open cold on the promise. This is the thesis — everything after pays it off.
90: 
91: ## Frame 2 — The problem
92: 
93: - scene: A 20-minute timer spins on a stack of rejected takes
94: - duration: 4s
95: - transition_in: crossfade
96: - status: built
97: - voiceover: "The old way? Prompt, wait twenty minutes, get something that misses."
98: - src: compositions/frames/02-problem.html
99: 
100: The old way: prompt, wait, get something that misses. Establish the pain we remove.
101: ```
102: 
103: ## Notes
104: 
105: - A frame with `status: outline` and no built `src` renders as an outline placeholder.
106: - `built` is the middle rung: the frame's HTML exists and its **layout is confirmed** (a wireframe sketch or better) — motion not yet added. Nothing is drawn yet beyond the approved layout.
107: - Multi-line `voiceover` values collapse to one line on save.

1: # The spec
2: 
3: Adjectives are where the default look lives. Given "premium, modern, clean", the model fills every gap with its own defaults, and they look the same in every run: a dark void, a glow, small type floating in the middle, everything fading in. Every adjective you turn into a number is a decision taken back from those defaults.
4: 
5: So before any scene, write `SPEC.md` at the project root: the film as a director's brief to yourself, with a number wherever you would have written an adjective. Build from it, check against it, and change it when a review changes the film.
6: 
7: The spec serves the story, never the other way round (`story.md`). A look that turns the story's things into abstract shapes has failed, however striking the frame.
8: 
9: ## The template
10: 
11: ```text
12: GOAL:    what the viewer feels or does at the end, one sentence
13: OUTPUT:  HyperFrames, W x H, fps
14: TIME:    seconds x fps = frames; BPM and frames per beat when there is music
15: LOOK:    ground (hex, texture and its amount), ink, one accent and where it may appear;
16:          display face + weight + size in px + tracking, body face the same;
17:          the medium (paper and ink, photographs, product UI, glass, clay, 3D studio) with its numbers;
18:          light and depth: shadow offset, blur and opacity, grain %, vignette %
19: OBJECTS: every thing the story needs the viewer to recognise (a mirror, a clock, a phone, a person),
20:          drawn with the material and details that make it read without a label: a mirror is
21:          silvered glass with a bright edge and a mount, not a bar
22: MOTION:  eases by role as named curves (enter, move, exit, camera); springs as damping ratio;
23:          durations and staggers in frames
24: SHOTS:   one line per shot: frame range, the one hero move, what the viewer reads (with its window),
25:          the sound, and how it hands off to the next shot
26: BANNED:  the defaults below, plus anything this film must not become
27: QA:      the frames to check, and what each must show
28: ```
29: 
30: ## Turning words into numbers
31: 
32: | The word  | Becomes                                                                                                                                |
33: | --------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
34: | premium   | a material with numbers: satin paper with 2% grain, a product on a seamless sweep with a 0.55 contact shadow, chrome at roughness 0.05 |
35: | modern    | a camera and a type system: a 30-frame push on one ease, a display face at 9% of the frame height with -2% tracking                    |
36: | clean     | a grid and a ration: 12 columns, 96 px margins, the accent on one word per shot                                                        |
37: | dynamic   | cuts on the beat, a layout change on the bar (every 4 beats), one hero move per shot                                                   |
38: | playful   | springs at damping 0.45-0.6 on position and scale (never on opacity or colour), 10-30% exaggerated poses                               |
39: | cinematic | a lens and a light: a 35 mm framing, a key from upper left, a rim from behind, 6% vignette                                             |
40: 
41: ## Composition numbers
42: 
43: - The hero of a shot fills at least 40% of the frame's height or width. A small object in the middle of an empty frame is never a shot; push in, crop, or give it a world.
44: - One hero move per shot. Secondary moves travel 50-70% as far, start 100-200 ms after it, and everything else holds still.
45: - In a story film every shot moves the story: something happens that causes the next shot. Lines read as cause and effect ("so…", "which means…"), not slogans.
46: - An information card (B-roll over a talking head, a data beat, a vertical explainer card) is different: its information is on screen within about 2.5 s, then it holds, so any paused frame reads as a finished poster.
47: - Something new every 2-4 s across the film; a new layout every bar when there is music.
48: - Text meant to be read: at least 28 px at 1080 (2.6% of the short side), held 0.5 s + 0.3 s a word. Too many words: cut words, never shrink type.
49: 
50: ## BANNED by default
51: 
52: These are where generated video lands when nothing else is decided. Each is banned unless the brand's own material or the person's reference uses it, and then only as they use it:
53: 
54: - a black or dark navy void as the ground, with small elements floating in its middle;
55: - glow, bloom, neon, lens flares, glowing orbs and rings; floating particles as decoration;
56: - purple or blue gradients, mesh gradients, glass cards;
57: - a cream or off-white paper ground with a serif display, italic accent words, numbered "01 / 02" labels, small monospace caps labels, pill-shaped chips and buttons;
58: - everything centred; everything fading in at once; every element fading and sliding up;
59: - text that moves while it is read; titles that keep drifting after they land;
60: - corner labels, frame borders, corner brackets, HUD readouts as decoration;
61: - three cards in a row, KPI grids, a title over a dimmed screenshot;
62: - the logo docked in a corner.
63: 
64: After the first render, name every default it used anyway, from this list or not, add each to the film's BANNED line, and fix them. The list grows with every film.
65: 
66: ## A look built from a medium
67: 
68: A look holds together when it is the rules of one medium, not a palette. A risograph look, for example, is five parts and nothing else:
69: 
70: - **paper**: one flat colour with a fibre noise, no gradients;
71: - **ink A**: every word that must be read and every structural line;
72: - **ink B**: one fluorescent accent, one focus per frame (the number, the bar, the stamp);
73: - **overprint**: where the inks overlap a third colour appears, and the B plate sits 3 px off register;
74: - **halftone**: every gradient is dots.
75: 
76: Motion comes from the same medium: the frame is printed, plate by plate, not faded in. Write any look this way: its parts, what each may carry, and how the medium itself moves (paper is cut and lifted, ink is printed, glass refracts, clay is pressed).

OUTPUT: HyperFrames · 1920×1080 · 30 fps · 46 s (1380 frames) · H.264 master, audio estéreo.

TIME: 100 BPM · 18 frames por pulso · corte cada 2–4 s · VO 150–160 wpm · pausas 0.3–0.5 s.

LOOK:

El video empieza en la pregunta, no en el producto. El caret es el primer trazo del hilo dorado y la carretera del logo es su primera forma.

- act: Acto 1 — La conversación

## Frame 3: El descubrimiento (10–17s)

- act: Acto 2 — El viaje

- status: built

- reads: "el titular se lee (10.6–12.4s); Hotel Plaza Neiva se lee (12.4–14.2s); Tatacoa 360° se lee (14.2–16.8s)"
- sound: "pins con pops secos; whoosh de mapa; la música sube"
- src: compositions/03-discovery.html

El mapa no es decoración: es la respuesta de la IA hecha espacio. Cada tarjeta es un lugar reconocible, no un pin genérico.

## Frame 4: La reserva (17–22.5s)

## Objective
- Globally install the HyperFrames skill, then produce the ViaNovaIA ~46 s Spanish-Colombian ad from `docs/PROMPT_VIDEO_HYPERFRAMES.md` in storyboard-first mode.
- Get approval on the 8-frame storyboard before animating, recording VO, mixing audio, or rendering deliverables.

## Requirements
- Use the prompt exactly: 16:9 1920×1080, 30 fps, ~45 s, warm cinematic tone, gold-thread concept, real ViaNova UI.
- Storyboard first: pose stills, snapshot them, build `boards/storyboard.html`, stop for approval.
- Deliverables: H.264 MP4 master, Spanish SRT, 1280×720 cover, three approval stills, optional 9:16 cut.
- Use only exact on-screen copy from the brief; do not invent claims, metrics, testimonials, or features.
- Never present the European lake hero as Colombia; never show QA/user names such as “QA Playwright”, “Visual Check”, or “José David Correa Núñez”.
- Approval stills required at 00:02, 00:20, 00:43.

## Decisions
- HyperFrames core skills installed globally at `C:\Users\Famil\.agents\skills`; `hyperframes`, `hyperframes-cli`, `hyperframes-registry` loaded.
- Project created at `video-vianova` with 8 sub-compositions and 8 storyboard frames at `2,7,14,20,25,30,36,43`.
- Rebuilt chat/dashboard UI in HTML instead of using screenshots with personal data or empty QA states.
- Visual system: `#FFBF00`, `#0B0B0C`, `#F5F4F0`, Poppins ExtraBold headlines, Inter UI, liquid glass, gold thread, grain/vignette.
- Used real Tatacoa photo and generated QR to `https://via-nova-ia.vercel.app`.
- Removed the black logo background by mapping near-black pixels to pure black; original preserved as `assets/img/logo-original.png`.
- Cropped `hotel-cabin.jpg` to a clean cabin-detail crop; removed the “Qué plan tan bonito” testimonial-style comment and used “Ruta guardada en tu itinerario.”
- Storyboard board uses wide frames for the voice scene and closing; acts are La conversación / El viaje / La vida local / El cierre.

## Work State
### Completed
- Global HyperFrames skills installed and loaded.
- `video-vianova` scaffolded; all 8 scenes written: `01-opening` through `08-closing`.
- `SPEC.md`, `STORYBOARD.md`, and `boards/storyboard.html` written.
- All 8 stills snapshotted to `boards/stills/`; every still visually inspected and layout issues fixed.
- Final `npx hyperframes check --json` passed: `ok: true`, 0 errors, lint 0 warnings; 46 contrast warnings and 16 craft warnings remain expected for static UI mockups, audio info only.
- `boards/.film.html` and `boards/.posed.html` created; film copy restored over `index.html` after posing.
- Board visually verified with Playwright.

### Active
- Present the approved storyboard board to the user and wait for their go.
- Answer the user’s open question: “Explica que esta sucediendo con el socket”.
